question.:question/problem:
![](images/86/86d6eae2f6bec9ef31d993d09aa56cbca88432678e10e3fa8b4ef72b4058077b.png)

The equation of the line $l_{1}$ is $y =-x + 3$ and the line $l_{2}$ is parallel to $l_{1}$. What is the equation of $l_{2}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line

$$
y = -x + 3
$$

The slope of the line

$$
y = -x + 3
$$

is

$$
-1
$$

So, we want a line with the slope $-1$ that passes through the point $(0,-1)$. Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - (-1) &= -1(x - (0)) \\
y &= -x + (-1) \\
y &= -x - 1
\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: x,y real; m nonzero finite rational

Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line

$$
y = \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{1}{3}
$$

The slope of the line

$$
y = \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{1}{3}
$$

is

$$
\frac{2}{3}
$$

So, we want a line with the slope $\frac{2}{3}$ that passes through the point $(-2,-3)$. Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - (-3) &= \frac{2}{3}(x - (-2)) \\
y &= \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{4}{3} + (-3) \\
y &= \frac{2}{3}x - \frac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 1

y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 1

$$
\begin{aligned}
y - y_{1} &= m(x - x_{1}) \\
y - (5) &= -\frac{3}{2}(x - (-4)) \\
y &= -\frac{3}{2}x - 6 + (5) \\

\end{aligned}
